content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces a set of text-classification models that use the GAT to model various hierarchies. Word-embeddings are used to compute a word's embedding. at the sentence level, the constituent word n-gram is used to construct a word-word graph. And finally the sentences in a sample are considered as nodes for the next level in the hierarchy. A straightforward graph construction mechanism is shown. Ablation studies show that the multi-level hierarchy is indeed useful (as opposed to throwing away those hierarchies).

There are an incomplete set of baselines compared against. In particular, the extremely strong GCN baselines from Lin et. al. 2021 have been left out in this paper for a reason that is not technically sound.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I would say in its current form, I feel the paper is incomplete and offers very little value to the NLP community. Very strong baselines from the prior art have been discarded due to lack of sufficient time and in a paper that is purely empirical, it isn't clear how that is a good enough reason. I would take the time to finish the work, try to match or improve upon the baselines and resubmit. 

Particular weaknesses start with the presentation. One, I feel you need a couple more passes at describing the hierarchy - maybe by using a small example diagram. It is a straightforward architecture that is described in a very verbose and ineffective way.

Next, you need to conduct multiple passes at describing the time-complexity. The writing is very casual and of a low quality. If space is an issue, please move the full analysis to supplementary material and only mention it here. 

Finally, I want to impress upon the authors that text classification is a _very fundamental_ NLP task. When you submit an empirical paper purely focused on this problem, incomplete work only hurts your paper's chances of success.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors promise to release code and the baselines are already public. So presumably the work is going to be reproducible.

I would content that a multi-hierarchical model for text is not that new an idea and similar efforts have existed for a long time. If the paper's claim is that this particular way of doing things is superior, then we need to see clear empirical evidence of that which we don't have.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- Incomplete work, selectively chosen baselines that aren't good enough.
- Overly verbose presentation style and writing that fails to communicate a fairly straightforward model.
- Insufficient technical value demonstrated in the current draft.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new approach, hierarchical graph neural network (HieGNN), which uses graph neural networks (GNNs) for semantic extraction from three levels: word-level, sentence-level, and document-level, to perform the text classification. The solution is based on the graph attention network (GAT) framework to gradually build HieGNN without modifying the original GAT formula.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The use of three-level graphs to build the HieGNN method is somewhat novel in GNN-based text classification studies. 
* Adapting the HieGNN architecture to a task set is simple and intuitive.
* It is great to see papers producing hierarchical methods for text classification. Of course, it would also be interesting to show the benefits of the proposed HieGNN over other datasets.

 
Weaknesses:

* One of the major drawbacks of this work is the paper title. The proposed method uses three separate graphs (word-level, sentence-level, and document-level) and merges these graphs' representations rather than handling a hierarchical approach (word-level input -> sentence-level input -> document-level input).
* The use of the HieGNN is insufficiently motivated. It is unclear what the benefit of using a graph representation to model this data is and why not existing Transformer language models handles different linguistic property across layers and maintain layer hierarchy. Should the model consider to be particularly suitable for text classification tasks? It would be nice if the authors could discuss why their method is beneficial for the chosen setting.
* The experimental section is weak, and hard to interpret the model training details.
* It is unclear how the proposed HieGNN differs from prior work. Prior work, such as Yao et al. (2019), also uses word and sentence-level graphs, which are constructed similarly. The authors should clearly describe how their model differs from prior approaches. If the main difference is the use of the three-level graphs, then this should be ablated to demonstrate its impact. As it is, there is insufficient analysis demonstrating which graph-level models are important.
* The new model is evaluated on several datasets, so it remains unclear whether the model truly outperforms prior models or whether its strong performance is due to having been tuned more extensively for these datasets. The model should be evaluated on standard GLUE tasks for comparability.
* What are the different linguistic properties captured across different levels of hierarchy?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The experimental section is weak, and hard to interpret the model training details.
* The writing style could be improved.
* Novelty of the work is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The most significant changes seem to be:
* details regarding the experimental setup and model training details 
* clarifications and details regarding graph construction at three levels and the HieGNN architecture
* a convincing motivation for using this architecture and this specific graph structure in relationship with the task at hand
* a more convincing validation of the main claim regarding the benefits of HieGNN training, including ablation studies
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
